cue.topic: Describe a time when you were very busy
bullets: and explain how you felt about it afterwards

part2.model: I'd like to talk about the month before my final exams at university, which was easily the busiest period of my life. It happened last May, when I had a dissertation deadline, three exams and a part-time job at a café all at once. On top of that, I had agreed to help organise a charity fundraiser for our student society. My supervisor, Dr Hargreaves, warned me that I was spreading myself too thin, but I stubbornly believed I could handle everything. For weeks I was running around like a headless chicken, getting up at six and rarely getting to bed before one. I lived on coffee and cereal bars, and I barely saw my friends. The reason I was so swamped was partly my own fault, because I'd left the dissertation until the last minute. Eventually I drew up a strict timetable, turned my phone off while studying and learned to say no to extra shifts. That finally got me back on track. Looking back, it was exhausting but strangely satisfying. When I handed in the dissertation with an hour to spare, I felt a huge wave of relief, and the fundraiser raised more than we had expected. I was burnt out for a few days afterwards, but that experience taught me to plan ahead, and I haven't left anything to the last minute since.

questions.q: Should employers be required by law to limit the hours their staff work?

A sensible compromise would be a weekly maximum with some flexibility, together with penalties for companies that pressure staff to work unpaid extra hours. Without such protection, workers could easily be taken advantage of.

questions.q: What might companies do to help employees maintain a healthy work-life balance?
questions.model: Firms could start by offering flexible schedules, so that parents and carers can fit work around family commitments. Generous annual leave also helps staff recharge, and managers should lead by example by actually taking their holidays. Some companies run wellbeing workshops, which are a nice gesture, but they achieve little if employees are still buried under unrealistic workloads. Real change begins with realistic targets and a culture of trust, because staff who feel respected are usually more productive anyway.
